## 1. What you'll build, and why

Concept 11 let you *build* an enum value but not look inside it — you could ask "are these the same
case?" but not "what's the radius of this circle?". That question — "*if* this is a `.circle`, give me
its `Int`" — is a **pattern**, and `switch` is how Swift asks it. Pattern matching reads which case a
value is, **binds its associated values**, runs the matching arm, and (this is the safety net)
**checks that you covered every case**. With it, the tagged unions from concept 11 finally become the
**algebraic data types** that make Swift expressive — and a little interpreter over an enum runs and
matches swiftc.

- **You implement:** the `switch` **dispatch lowering** in SILGen, and the **exhaustiveness** check in
  sema.
- **Outcome:** `switch` programs **run and match swiftc** — destructuring, an ADT evaluator, `Int`
  switches.

## 2. Concepts in depth

### A switch is a dispatch on the tag

Once an enum is a tag + payload (concept 11), `switch` almost writes itself: read the **tag**, then
test it against each case; on a match, **pull the payload out** and run that arm. It compiles to a
chain of conditional branches:

![Lowering `switch`: read the tag with `enum_tag`, then a chain of `tag == k ?` tests; each true edge goes to a case block that binds the payload (`enum_payload`) and runs the body; all case blocks join at a merge. An exhaustive enum switch ends the chain in `unreachable`.](figs/dispatch.png)

It's the same block-building you did for `if`/`while` in concept 08, in a new shape: evaluate the
subject **once**, derive the discriminant (`enum_tag` for an enum, the value itself for an `Int`), make
a `merge` block, and walk the cases — each one emits `key = tag`, `cond_br (disc == key)` to a fresh
*case block* or a fresh *next-test block*. The case block binds, runs its body, and branches to merge.
The chain's final fall-through is the `default` body, or — for an exhaustive enum switch — `unreachable`
(control provably never gets there).

### Binding a payload *is* a `let`

`case .circle(let r):` binds `r` to the circle's associated value. In the case block you know the tag,
so it's now **safe** to read the payload (you'd never read `rect`'s second field out of a `circle`).
Each `let x` lowers exactly like a local binding: `enum_payload subj #i` reads the slot, then
`alloc_stack x` + `store` puts it in a variable, in scope for the arm's body. `_` ignores its slot.
That safety — you can only read a payload *after* the tag check routes you into the case — is the whole
reason associated values live behind `switch` and not behind plain field access.

### Exhaustiveness — the check that makes it safe

A `switch` over an enum **must handle every case** (or have a `default`). swiftc rejects a switch that
forgets one, and so do we: track which case names the patterns matched, and if any of the enum's cases
is left uncovered with no `default`, emit "switch must be exhaustive." This is more than pedantry — it's
what makes enums *refactorable*: add a case to the enum, and the compiler points you at every `switch`
that now needs updating. (`Int` switches can't be exhaustive — too many values — so they always need a
`default`.) Real swiftc proves exhaustiveness with a small algebra of "spaces"
(`TypeCheckSwitchStmt.cpp`); ours is the set-cover special case for flat enum patterns.

### A switch can also return

A function whose whole body is a `switch` returns a value *through* the switch:
`func area(_ s: Shape) -> Int { switch s { case …: return … } }`. So the **"missing return"** analysis
from concept 07 grows one rule: a `switch` is a definite return when **every** case body returns and
(the `default` returns, or there's no `default` and it's exhaustive — which sema already guaranteed).
Without that rule, every `switch`-bodied function would falsely report "missing return" — a bug worth
seeing, because it's the kind of cross-feature interaction that only shows up when you actually run a
realistic program.

### The subset you are growing into

**New lexemes.** Two keywords, both in `token.ml`'s `keyword_or_ident` table; `case` is
concept 11's, reused in a second place:

| spelling | token | notes |
|---|---|---|
| `switch` | `Token.Kw_switch` | a keyword — a statement, like `if` and `while` |
| `default` | `Token.Kw_default` | a keyword — the catch-all arm |
| `case` | `Token.Kw_case` | concept 11's keyword, now also opening a `switch` arm |

**The grammar** — `<-- new` marks what this concept adds; everything else is concepts 05–11.
Notation is EBNF: `[ x ]` is *optional* (zero or one), `{ x }` is *repetition* (zero or more),
`|` separates alternatives, and quoted text is a terminal.

```
statement   ::= switch_stmt                                        <-- new
              | ("let" | "var") ident [ ":" type ] "=" expr
              | ident "=" expr
              | ident "." ident "=" expr
              | "if" expr block [ "else" ( block | if-statement ) ]
              | "while" expr block
              | "for" ident "in" expr "..<" expr block
              | "break" | "continue" | "return" [ expr ]
              | expr

switch_stmt ::= "switch" expr "{" [ nl ] { arm } "}"               <-- new
arm         ::= "case" pattern ":" { statement NEWLINE }           <-- new
              | "default" ":" { statement NEWLINE }                <-- new
pattern     ::= "." ident [ "(" binding { "," binding } ")" ]      <-- new (an enum case)
              | [ "-" ] int                                        <-- new (an Int literal)
binding     ::= "let" ident | "_"                                  <-- new
nl          ::= NEWLINE { NEWLINE }   # one or more: a run of blank lines is one separator
```

Three things to notice. An arm's body is **not** a block: there are no braces, and the body runs
to the next `case`, `default` or `}` — which is why `parse_case_body` stops on those three tokens
instead of on a `}`. A pattern starts with a **leading dot** and no type name (`.circle`, not
`Shape.circle`): the subject's type is what says which enum it is, so the parser can commit on the
`.` alone and sema resolves the case. And a `binding` is `let x` or `_`, never a bare expression —
Swift's `case let x` and `case x where …` forms, and tuple and nested patterns, are the exercises.

### The diagnostics you emit (and the ones you are given)

One of these is yours: `switch must be exhaustive`, the `TODO(12-sema)` hole. The rest are given
and pinned by `sema-switch.t`, so you can rely on them — nothing ill-typed reaches your dispatch
chain. Wording follows `swiftc -typecheck` where the subset lets it
(`swift/include/swift/AST/DiagnosticsSema.def`, line numbers from the pinned snapshot).

| program | our message | swiftc |
|---|---|---|
| an enum switch missing a case, no `default` | **`switch must be exhaustive`** — *your hole* | **same** (`non_exhaustive_switch`, l.7771) — swiftc adds a fix-it listing the missing cases; we stop at the sentence |
| an `Int` switch with no `default` | `switch must be exhaustive` (given) | **same** — an `Int` has too many values to cover |
| `case .nope:` | `type 'Shape' has no member 'nope'` | **same** (`could_not_find_type_member`, l.86) |
| `case 1:` on an enum subject | `expression pattern of type 'Int' cannot match values of type 'E'` | **same** (`cannot_match_expr_pattern_with_value`, l.5602) |
| `case .a:` on an `Int` subject | `enum case '.a' cannot match values of type 'Int'` | `type 'Int' has no member 'a'` — swiftc resolves the pattern *first* and never gets to the match |
| `switch b` on a `Bool` | `cannot 'switch' over a value of type 'Bool'` | **accepted** — swiftc matches `true`/`false` patterns over any `Equatable`; our patterns are enum cases and `Int` literals only, so we say so rather than mis-lower it |
| `case .rect(let w)` for `case rect(Int, Int)` | `pattern '.rect' binds 1 value(s) but case 'rect' has 2 associated value(s)` | **accepted** — swiftc binds the whole `(Int, Int)` *tuple* to `w`. We have no tuple type, so we refuse rather than bind something we cannot represent |
| `print(r)` outside the arm that bound `r` | `cannot find 'r' in scope` | **same** (`cannot_find_in_scope`) — a binding is scoped to its arm |

### How a real compiler dispatches (and what we simplified)

Our dispatch is a **linear** chain: *n* cases cost up to *n* tag comparisons. A production compiler
builds a **decision tree** — a balanced binary search on the tag, or a **jump table** when the tags are
dense (which they are: 0, 1, 2, …). swiftc's SIL has a dedicated **`switch_enum`** terminator that
lowers straight to LLVM's `switch` instruction (a jump table). Same semantics, better asymptotics; the
linear chain is the honest, readable starting point, and turning it into a `switch_enum` is an exercise.

## 3. Build it, step by step

The parser is given (patterns, arms, `default`), and so is the pattern *typing* — by the time your
code runs, every pattern names a real case with the right number of bindings. Two holes:

- **`sema.ml`, `TODO(12-sema)` in `check_switch`** — EXHAUSTIVENESS. The enum branch already
  collects the case names the patterns matched into `covered`, and `el.Types.el_cases` is what the
  enum declares. When there is no `default` and something is left over, report it with swiftc's
  sentence, `switch must be exhaustive`, at the switch's own span. (The `Int` branch already does
  its half: an `Int` switch always needs a `default`.) `sema-exhaustive.t` is five programs swiftc
  refuses and the skeleton accepts.
- **`silgen.ml`, `TODO(12)`, the `Switch` arm of `gen_stmt`** — the DISPATCH CHAIN. Evaluate the
  subject **once**; the discriminant is its tag for an enum (`Sil.Enum_tag`) and the value itself
  for an `Int`. Then, per case: compare the discriminant with that pattern's key (the case's
  `Types.case_index`, or the literal), and `Cond_br` to a fresh block for the arm or to a fresh
  block that carries on testing. Inside an arm, a binding is an ordinary local — read the payload
  with `Sil.Enum_payload (subj, i)`, give it an `alloc_stack`, `store` it, and register it in
  `b.vars` — then generate the body and branch to the ONE merge block every arm shares. When the
  chain runs out: the `default` body if there is one, and otherwise `Sil.Unreachable`, because
  sema has just proved no case is left. End by switching to the merge block, so whatever follows
  the switch is generated there. `silgen-switch.t` prints the CFG you built.

Reference: `solution/` — after you have tried it.

## 4. Test it

```bash
make lab C=phase3-value-types/12-pattern-matching
```

Every `.t` file calls `./lab.exe`, built from **this directory's** library, so the report is about
your code here. In the order you fill the holes:

- `sema-switch.t` — `--typecheck`: the given pattern rules (binding arity, an unknown case, an
  `Int` pattern against an enum and the reverse, a `Bool` subject, a binding's arm-local scope and
  its type). Green from the start; it is the contract your lowering may rely on.
- `sema-exhaustive.t` — `--typecheck`, the sema hole: five enum switches that leave a case
  uncovered — one of two, two of three, the same case listed twice, an empty switch, and one
  inside a function. Every one of them is accepted by the skeleton, so the file is `TODO` until
  the check exists.
- `silgen-switch.t` — `--emit-sil`, the silgen hole: the whole dispatch chain of a three-case
  switch, the single `enum_tag`, `enum_payload … #0`/`#1` per arm, `_` extracting nothing, a
  switch used as a statement (the arms `br` to the merge), an `Int` switch with a `default`, and
  a `default` replacing the trailing `unreachable`.
- `run-switch.t` — `build` and run: destructuring, an `Op` interpreter, a switch as a statement,
  an `Int` switch with `default`, a switch in a loop, and a `default` arm. It needs the silgen
  hole only — the sema hole adds a rejection, not a behaviour.
- `test_switch.ml` (alcotest `switch`) — the same three groups in-process: `sema-switch` (given —
  its three cases pass on the skeleton), `sema-exhaustive`, `silgen-switch`.
- `oracle.t` — **the headline**, in two halves. The runtime half compiles the 16 programs of
  `oracle-corpus.txt` with `swiftc -Onone` and with `./lab.exe build`, runs both binaries, and
  demands identical stdout and exit code. The front-end half asks `swiftc -typecheck` and
  `./lab.exe --typecheck` for a verdict on the 15 programs of `typecheck-corpus.txt` — five
  well-formed, ten refused, five of those for exhaustiveness — and they must agree. That half is
  the only oracle the sema hole has, so it stays red until the check is written.

A hole you have not started shows as `TODO` with the list of what it will check; a hole in
progress shows `FAIL` with, under each failing case, what the test wants and what your code
printed. On the untouched skeleton `sema-switch.t` is `PASS` and everything else is `TODO`, with
the alcotest `FAIL` and its three `sema-switch` cases `OK`.

## 5. Benchmark it

Time a `switch` with many cases against swiftc. Our linear chain is O(cases); swiftc's jump table is
O(1). For a hot interpreter loop that's a real gap — and exactly what Exercise 4 (a `switch_enum`
terminator → LLVM `switch`) closes.

## 6. Exercises

1. **`where` clauses.** `case .circle(let r) where r > 0:` — after binding, evaluate the guard and
   `cond_br` on it (match only if the pattern *and* the guard hold; otherwise fall to the next test).
2. **`if let` / `guard let`.** `if case .circle(let r) = shape { … }` is a one-case switch; `guard`
   binds into the *enclosing* scope and `else`-returns. Desugar both to the dispatch you just built.
3. **Tuple & nested patterns.** `switch (a, b) { case (0, let y): … }` — match a tuple position-wise,
   recursing the matcher into sub-patterns. The space algebra generalizes exhaustiveness to these.
4. **`switch_enum` (jump table).** Add a `Switch_enum of value * (int * int) list * int option`
   terminator (tag → block, plus default) and lower it to LLVM's `switch`. Replace the linear chain;
   measure the speedup.

## 7. Recap & what's next

You added `switch`: a tag dispatch that binds associated values and is checked **exhaustive**. Enums
are now first-class — you can take them apart, and a tree of cases is an interpreter. That's the ADT
half of Phase 3 complete.

Next, **13-optionals**, where a beautiful thing happens: `Optional<T>` turns out to be *just an enum* —
`enum Optional<T> { case none; case some(T) }` — so `nil`, `?`, `!`, `if let`, and `??` are all built
on the enum + pattern-matching machinery you now have. The sugar is new; the engine is done.

## 8. Appendix — full solution

From `solution/silgen.ml` (dispatch) and `solution/sema.ml` (exhaustiveness):

```ocaml
| Ast.Switch { subject; cases; default; _ } ->
    let subj = gen_expr b subject in
    let enum_name = match vty b subj with Types.TEnum en -> Some en | _ -> None in
    let disc = match enum_name with Some _ -> emit b (Sil.Enum_tag subj) Types.TInt | None -> subj in
    let merge = new_block b in
    let key_of = function
      | Ast.PEnumCase (cn, _) ->
          let el = Hashtbl.find b.enums (Option.get enum_name) in
          Option.get (Types.case_index el cn)
      | Ast.PInt n -> n in
    let bind_payload = function
      | Ast.PEnumCase (cn, bindings) when enum_name <> None ->
          let tys = Option.get (Types.case_payload (Hashtbl.find b.enums (Option.get enum_name)) cn) in
          List.iteri (fun i bnd -> match bnd with
            | Ast.Bind x ->
                let pv = emit b (Sil.Enum_payload (subj, i)) (List.nth tys i) in
                let addr = emit b (Sil.Alloc_stack x) (vty b pv) in
                Hashtbl.replace b.vars x addr; ignore (emit b (Sil.Store (pv, addr)) Types.TVoid)
            | Ast.Ignore -> ()) bindings
      | _ -> () in
    let rec dispatch = function
      | [] -> (match default with
          | Some body -> gen_block b body; terminate b (Sil.Br merge.Sil.bid)
          | None -> terminate b Sil.Unreachable)
      | (pat, body) :: rest ->
          let k = emit b (Sil.Int_lit (key_of pat)) Types.TInt in
          let c = emit b (Sil.Binop (Ast.Eq, disc, k)) Types.TBool in
          let case_b = new_block b and next_b = new_block b in
          terminate b (Sil.Cond_br (c, case_b.Sil.bid, next_b.Sil.bid));
          switch_to b case_b; bind_payload pat; gen_block b body; terminate b (Sil.Br merge.Sil.bid);
          switch_to b next_b; dispatch rest in
    dispatch cases; switch_to b merge
```

```ocaml
(* sema: exhaustiveness — no default ⇒ every case must be covered *)
Option.iter check_block default;
if default = None then begin
  let missing = List.filter (fun (c, _) -> not (List.mem c !covered)) el.Types.el_cases in
  if missing <> [] then err span "switch must be exhaustive"
end
```

## 9. Exercise solutions

### 1 — `where` clauses

Give a case an optional guard expression. After `bind_payload`, `gen_expr` the guard and `cond_br` on
it: true → the body (→ merge), false → the *next* test block (so a guarded pattern that fails tries the
following case). In sema, a `where`-guarded case does **not** count toward exhaustiveness (it might not
match), so swiftc still requires a `default` — match that.

### 2 — `if let` / `guard let`

`if case .some(let x) = opt { … } else { … }` is a two-arm switch (the case, and an implicit default).
`guard case .some(let x) = opt else { return }` binds `x` into the **enclosing** scope (not a nested
block) and requires the `else` to exit. Both desugar to the same `enum_tag` + `cond_br` + `enum_payload`
you built — which is exactly why concept 13 gets optionals "for free."

### 3 — tuple & nested patterns

Represent patterns recursively (`PTuple of pattern list`, `PEnumCase of string * pattern list`). The
matcher becomes recursive: test the outer tag/shape, then match each sub-pattern against the
corresponding payload slot, binding as it descends. Exhaustiveness generalizes to a **product/sum
space** algebra — the real `TypeCheckSwitchStmt` algorithm.

### 4 — `switch_enum` terminator

Add `Switch_enum of value * (int * int) list * int option` (discriminant, (tag → block) list, optional
default block). Build all case blocks first, then emit one terminator; lower it to LLVM
`switch i64 %t, label %default [ i64 0, label %bb0  i64 1, label %bb1 … ]` — a jump table. O(1) dispatch
regardless of case count, and the shape swiftc actually emits.
```
